attributes.title: Level 4

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: set up, player sprite code, moving sprite code, sprite overlap code.


Start each comment with //﻿ and add several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓Did you rename both sprites using camelCase and select an image for each?
steps.instructions:
Add 2 sprites to the project! 


Open Sprites then drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] under // player sprite code


Click the palette to select a sprite, then replace mySprite with a simple name using camelCase that describes what it is, such as playerSprite


Repeat the same steps to create another sprite under  // moving sprite code


Click ▶ to see the 2 sprites appear in the center of the screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you replace mySprite with the name of the player sprite in controller.moveSprite(sprite)?
steps.instructions:
Set the player sprite’s starting position and on screen movement.


Open Sprites, drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] onto a blank line under the existing code under // player sprite code. Update the sprite’s name and the x (0-160) and y (0-120) parameters so that the sprite appears on the left side of the screen.


Open Controller and drag [move (mySprite) with buttons] underneath the line of code that sets the player sprite’s position. Inside the parentheses, replace mySprite with the name of the player sprite.


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) stay in screen (true)] underneath the line of code that moves the player sprite with buttons. Update the player sprite’s name, and use the default argument true so the sprite will stay in screen.


Click ▶ to move the player sprite around the screen and notice how it stays in screen.

steps.hints: ❓Did you update the x and y parameters inside the parentheses of setPosition so that  randint is used to select a coordinate from a range of values?
steps.instructions:
Make the moving sprite appear in random positions on the screen every half second!


Open Game and drag [run code on game update every (period) ms] underneath the existing code under // moving sprite code


Open Sprites, drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] inside the curly brackets { } of game.onUpdateInterval. Update the moving sprite’s name.


Open Math and drag [randint] to replace the first parameter inside the parentheses of setPosition. Keep the minimum value at 0 and replace the maximum value 10 by typing screen.width to select a random x value between 0 and 160. 


Drag another [randint] to replace the second parameter inside the parentheses of setPosition. Keep the minimum value at 0 and replace the maximum value 10 by typing screen.height to select a random y value between 0 and 120. 


Click ▶ to see the moving sprite appear at random places on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you put the  if conditional inside the curly brackets of the forever loop?
steps.instructions:
Code something to happen when the player and the moving sprite overlap! 


Open Loops and drag [run code forever] under // sprite overlap code. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

forever(function() {...})

Open Logic and drag [if] inside the curly brackets { } of the forever loop. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text

if (true) {...}

The if conditional acts as a block statement nested inside the curly brackets of the forever loop. It is indented and contains its own set of curly brackets { } to place code inside of.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace true inside the parentheses of the if condition with mySprite.overlapsWith(otherSprite)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What condition needs to be true, in order for the gameOver function to run?

❓ Why should the gameOver code be placed inside the curly brackets { } of the if conditional? What would happen if it was simply placed inside the curly brackets { } of the forever loop?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that since the overlapsWith code is checking if two sprites have overlapped, it does not matter the order in which the names of the sprites are placed in the code.

💡 Explain the logic of the code to the ninja: throughout the project, if the player sprite has overlapped with the moving sprite, then the game will end in a loss. Else, the code will not run and the game will continue. 

💡 Help the ninja notice how the if conditional is nested inside of the forever loop and has its own set of curly brackets. In order for the gameOver code to run when a certain condition is true, it must be placed inside the curly brackets of the if conditional.
steps.instructions:
Add a Boolean for the conditional to check, and end the game if the Boolean is true!


Delete true inside the parentheses of the if condition. Open Sprites and drag [(mySprite) overlaps with (otherSprite)] inside the parentheses. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

mySprite.overlapsWith(otherSprite)


Replace mySprite with the name of the player sprite and otherSprite with the name of the moving sprite.


Open Game again and drag [game over (true)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if condition. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:

game.gameOver(true)


The gameOver function has 1 parameter: win. Change the win parameter to false, to end the game in a loss.


Click ▶ to see the game end if the 2 sprites overlap.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you place the setGameOverEffect function above the gameOver function, inside the if condition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the setGameOverEffect function be placed above the gameOver function? 

❓ What effect might run when the game ends in a loss?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja the importance of sequence in their code. Similarly to setting the dialog frame’s image before displaying a dialog box on screen, the game over effect must be set before the game over function is run. Otherwise, the effect will not apply to the game over screen.

💡 Assist the Ninja with placing the setGameOverEffect function in the correct location. It may appear on the line below (due to a MakeCode bug). Remind the Ninja that they can use CTRL + X/V to cut then paste the function into the correct spot.

💡 Encourage the ninja to test out different effects in the code completion tool to match with the game over condition. Note that not all effects listed in the code completion tool can be used as a screen (game over) effect.
steps.instructions:
Customize the game over screen with an effect!


Open Game and drag [use effect (effects.confetti) for (true)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if condition, above the gameOver function. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text: 

game.setGameOverEffect(true, effects.confetti)

The setGameOverEffect function has 2 possible parameters: win and effect. Change the win parameter to false. In the effect parameter, delete .confetti, then retype the dot operator . and select an effect to run when the game ends in a loss.


Click ▶ to see an effect run when the game ends.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type a number between 1-15 to set the color parameter in the parentheses in scene.setBackgroundColor(color)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What background color might you use as a backdrop for the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can always click on the palette for one of the images in the code to open the editor. Once opened, they can hover their cursor over each individual color to find the corresponding value to use as a background color.

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background color and directions!


Open Scene, then drag [set background color to (color)] under // set up. Inside the parentheses, replace 0 with a number between 1-15 to set the background color. 


Open Game, drag out [splash (title)] under // set up. Replace null with a string inside of quotation marks that provides game directions.


Click ▶ to see the background color appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you switch back to the blocks editor? What looks similar and what looks different?
steps.instructions:
Test out the project. Does it work as expected?


Switch to the blocks editor to see what the JavaScript code looks like in blocks! Notice what is similar about the code, and what looks different: how do the nested block statements inside the curly brackets appear in blocks, versus in JavaScript?

subgroups.title: Save the Crab!
subgroups.introduction: Create a project in JavaScript that uses conditionals and nested block statements.

validationItems.text: Use 1 sprite with a custom name and set its position, move it with the controller, and keep it in the screen.
Use 1 sprite with a custom name and set its position to a random value inside an onUpdateInterval function.
Use a forever loop with an if conditional statement inside.
Use the overlapsWith function to determine when the game is over. Use a custom game over effect.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 4 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about conditionals and nested block statements. Nested block statements are created when code inside of curly brackets is placed inside of another chunk of code in curly brackets, such as placing a conditional inside of a forever loop. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 4:

badges.title: Curly Brackets All the Way Down
badges.description: Use nested block statements to place one block statement inside another in JavaScript.

badges.title: If at First You Don’t Succeed
badges.description: Use  “if” and “if / else” statements in JavaScript.

badges.title: ...or Else
badges.description: Use an “else if” statement in JavaScript.

badges.title: Until the End of Time
badges.description: Use a forever loop in JavaScript.

badges.title: Hey I’m Walking Here
badges.description: Use the overlapsWith function to see if two sprites are overlapping.

badges.title: Gaming the System
badges.description: Use the setGameOverEffect and gameOver functions to customize game over screens.

badges.title: The Final Countdown
badges.description: Use the info.onCountdownEnd function to run code when the countdown reaches zero.

badges.title: Playing the Odds
badges.description: Use the Math.percentChance function inside an if statement to add randomness to a project.

badges.title: A Flair for the Dramatic
badges.description: Add a custom sprite effect to a sprite.

badges.title: Let’s Try That Again
badges.description: Use the game.reset function to restart a project.
